performers: Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord; Advent Chamber Orchestra
intro: The second movement, Affettuoso, of the Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050, is scored for flute, violin and harpsichord alone, with the orchestra silent. The three instruments exchange dotted phrases in B minor, and the harpsichord plays both the bass line and solo passages.

sections.label: A · Violin and flute in B minor
sections.mNote: Dotted phrases pass between the three soloists.

sections.label: B · Flute refrain in F♯ minor
sections.mNote: The harpsichord follows the flute’s four-bar refrain.

sections.label: C · Refrain in G major, then keyboard
sections.mNote: A varied refrain precedes the longest keyboard solo.

sections.label: A′ · B minor, violin leading
sections.mNote: The violin plays the opening phrase again.

cues.title: Flute, violin and harpsichord
cues.text: The violin begins and the flute follows. Under their dotted phrases the harpsichord plays a walking bass line, then adds its right hand as a third melodic part. The accompanying strings rest for the whole movement.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871), II, pp. 149–151: flute, solo violin and harpsichord only. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ed/IMSLP02043-BWV1050.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to the Margrave, 1721
cues.text: On 24 March 1721 Bach dated the dedication of six concertos to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg. Each concerto calls for a different group of players. This one sets a flute beside a violin and a harpsichord.
cues.evidence: The dedication and the scoring are preserved in the 1721 presentation manuscript. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5

cues.title: Marking changed from Adagio to Affettuoso
cues.text: The earlier version of this concerto marks the movement Adagio. In the 1721 score for the Margrave, Bach changed the marking to Affettuoso (tenderly, with feeling). Flute, violin and harpsichord play the movement without the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Neue Bach-Ausgabe VII/2 (Nachtrag), ed. Alfred Dürr (Bärenreiter, 1975), BWV 1050a, p. 26: the second movement of the early version is headed “Adagio”, for flute, violin and harpsichord (IMSLP #828858). The Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 149, heads this movement Affettuoso.

cues.title: Third refrain in F♯ minor
cues.text: The refrain moves to F♯ minor. The flute leads and the violin follows. When the harpsichord takes over, its right hand keeps the dotted rhythm and decorates it while the left hand continues underneath.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 150: the third refrain and following keyboard episode.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Refrain in G major
cues.text: The refrain moves to G major. The flute leads again, and Bach alters the phrase before the harpsichord takes it over. The harpsichord’s passage that follows is the longest in the movement, with short interjections from flute and violin.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, pp. 150–151, fourth refrain and episode. The movement’s form is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violinist at Weimar, 1703
cues.text: In 1703 the eighteen-year-old Bach spent about half a year as a violinist in Duke Johann Ernst III’s private orchestra at Weimar. Later that year he took the post of organist in Arnstadt.

cues.title: Köthen and Leipzig, 1717–1723
cues.text: Bach signed his contract at Köthen in August 1717. As Thomaskantor in Leipzig from 1723 he owed the churches a cantata every Sunday and feast day, about sixty a year. Prince Leopold still commissioned a birthday cantata from him each year.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig, chronology, entries for 1717 and 1723. https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology

cues.title: Return of the opening phrase
cues.text: The violin plays the first phrase again in B minor, and the flute follows as at the start. The harpsichord’s right-hand solo ends, and its bass part supports the last exchange and the closing chord.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 151, final system: return of the opening refrain and B-minor cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Flute refrain returns in F♯ minor
transitions.from: A · Violin and flute in B minor
transitions.to: B · Flute refrain in F♯ minor
transitions.how: The harpsichord’s running right-hand line ends, and the flute brings back the dotted refrain in F♯ minor. The violin follows over the keyboard bass. Bach marks the returning solo lines forte, and the harpsichord goes back to accompanying.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 150, first and second systems: third refrain.

transitions.title: The refrain in G major
transitions.from: B · Flute refrain in F♯ minor
transitions.to: C · Refrain in G major, then keyboard
transitions.how: The flute and violin play the dotted phrase in G major, marked forte, and the keyboard plays the bass. This refrain is a variant of the opening melody. At its close the harpsichord’s right hand has another solo, and the flute and violin reply in short phrases.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, pp. 150–151: fourth refrain and final keyboard episode.

transitions.title: The violin returns to B minor
transitions.from: C · Refrain in G major, then keyboard
transitions.how: The extended keyboard solo ends. Over the harpsichord’s bass, the violin starts the opening B-minor refrain and the flute follows. Both solo lines are marked forte. For the final cadence the keyboard’s right hand plays accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 151, final system.

source.title: Bach, Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050 — Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871)
source.locator: II. Affettuoso, printed pp. 149–151: flute, solo violin and harpsichord alone. The dotted refrain passes through B minor, F♯ minor and G major before returning home.

timeline.note: Violin and flute exchange a dotted phrase over the harpsichord’s bass. The keyboard answers between their statements.
The flute begins the refrain in F♯ minor. The harpsichord answers with its written-out upper part.
The refrain reaches G major, followed by the longest keyboard reply. Violin and flute interrupt with their dotted phrase.
Violin and flute return to the opening exchange in B minor. The harpsichord accompanies them to the close.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
